Lower maximum prices may be seen as a positive for customers, but it comes with a tradeoff; the minimum hourly price for residential customers in the 2019 Mild scenario is only 4-6 cents lower than the median, with all Mild prices existing above the median value of the Full price. Moving to 2030, we see an increasing range of prices across all scenarios, including both higher maximums and lower minimums. Note that the prices shown in the figure and described here are in 2019 dollars, using a 2019-2030 inflation factor of 1.45. Figure 11 highlights how the ranges in prices shown above manifest in the daily price shape patterns. As expected, the Mild scenario has relatively flatter prices across the day, with the Full tariff showing a distinctive “duck curve” shape. Moving from 2019 to 2030, we see the belly of the duck deepen slightly, and particularly in the 2030 High scenario we see a very substantial range in the average daily price shape, with the average daytime price near $0.10/kWh and the average evening peak price nearing $0.70/kWh (in 2019 dollars). This illustrates how an increasingly renewable, and increasingly expensive, electricity grid can result in dramatic price swings that can enable significant savings from load flexibility. Figure 11. Average daily price shape for an illustrative customer class across price years, price forecast scenarios, and tariff design scenarios. Ultimately, the most important feature of a price profile is the difference in prices that can be capitalized on by shifting load. Generally, most end uses will shift load within a given day, and over the span of several hours. In order to illustrate this price saving opportunity, we therefore 25 calculate the average of (a) the lowest four hourly prices and (b) the highest four hourly prices in each day across the year. We then take the difference between those two values and refer to it here as the “daily price differential”. In Figure 12, we show the sorted values of those differentials across the year, for the 2030 low price forecast, for all utilities and tariff design scenarios. The top row of the figure is for residential customers, while the bottom row is for large C&I. This figure shows the significant difference in the tariff design scenarios; the Mild tariff differentials sit almost wholly below the Full and Medium values.
